nodes.label: Gamsakhurdia
nodes.full: Zviad Gamsakhurdia, a philologist and former dissident, was elected president on 26 May 1991 with about 87 per cent of the vote, and the Supreme Council had restored independence on 9 April. His nationalist rhetoric toward the minorities, his conflicts with the opposition and the National Guard and his authoritarian style led to a rebellion in Tbilisi in December 1991, and he fled the city on 6 January 1992. He returned in the west of the country in 1993 and died on 31 December 1993; the circumstances of his death are disputed.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (1991); Stephen Jones, Georgia: A Political History since Independence (2012); Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation (1994).

nodes.label: Shevardnadze
nodes.full: Eduard Shevardnadze, the former Soviet foreign minister, returned on 7 March 1992 at the invitation of the military council, was elected chairman of parliament on 11 October 1992, and was elected president in November 1995 and again in April 2000. He ended the civil war with Russian support and the entry into the CIS, stabilised the state, introduced the lari in 1995 and the constitution, and survived two assassination attempts, but his rule became increasingly corrupt, and he resigned on 23 November 2003 after the disputed parliamentary election.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records; Jones 2012; Shevardnadze, The Future Belongs to Freedom (1991).

nodes.label: Saakashvili
nodes.full: Mikheil Saakashvili, a US-trained lawyer and the leader of the United National Movement, was elected on 4 January 2004 with about 96 per cent and re-elected on 5 January 2008 with about 53 per cent. He led the reforms of the police and administration, the reintegration of Adjara, the war of 2008 and a close alignment with the United States; his critics point to the repression of November 2007 and the abuses of the prison system, and he left office in November 2013. After years in Ukraine he returned in October 2021 and was arrested, and he has been sentenced in several cases to a total of about twelve and a half years, which he and his supporters call political.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records; Jones 2012; Georgian court judgments (2021–2025); Al Jazeera and Civil.ge reports.

nodes.label: Margvelashvili
nodes.full: Giorgi Margvelashvili, a philosopher nominated by the Georgian Dream coalition, was elected in October 2013 and took office after the constitutional change which reduced the president's powers; his term was marked by the cohabitation with the government of the founder Bidzina Ivanishvili and his successors, and by tension with Ivanishvili in the last years. He did not run for a second term.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (2013); Constitution of Georgia (2010 amendments).

nodes.label: Zourabichvili
nodes.full: Salome Zourabichvili, a French-born diplomat and former foreign minister, was elected in the second round on 28 November 2018 with Georgian Dream's backing, as the last president elected by direct vote. She broke with the party over its turn from the West, vetoed the foreign-influence law of 2024 and the family-values law, and after the disputed elections of October 2024 declared the new parliament illegitimate; she left the presidential palace after the inauguration of her successor in December 2024 but says she is the country's legitimate president, which the authorities reject.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (2018); presidential statements (2024); Civil.ge reports.

nodes.label: Kavelashvili
nodes.full: Mikheil Kavelashvili, a former footballer and a founder of the People's Power group allied to Georgian Dream, was elected on 14 December 2024 by an electoral college of the parliament and local deputies, under the amended constitution of 2017, and was inaugurated on 29 December. The government regards the election as lawful; the opposition and Zourabichvili call it illegitimate because it followed the disputed elections and the boycott of the opposition. As of 2026 he is head of state.
nodes.src: Constitution of Georgia (2017 amendments); Central Electoral Commission and Civil.ge reports (December 2024).

nodes.label: Governments of the first republic
nodes.full: Under Shevardnadze the cabinets were led by prime ministers and state ministers such as Tengiz Sigua, Otar Patsatsia and Vazha Lortkipanidze; the parliament was chaired by the reformer Zurab Zhvania, who in 1999 told the Council of Europe that he was a Georgian and therefore a European. The governments were unable to collect taxes or to pay the pensions and salaries, and their ministers were often accused of corruption.
nodes.src: Government and parliamentary records; Jones 2012.

nodes.label: Governments of the UNM
nodes.full: The prime ministers of the Saakashvili years were Zurab Zhvania (2004–2005, who died on 3 February 2005 of carbon monoxide poisoning), Zurab Noghaideli, Lado Gurgenidze, Nika Gilauri and, briefly, Vano Merabishvili; they carried out the reforms of the police, taxes and customs and were accused of concentrating power in the presidency.
nodes.src: Government records; Jones 2012; Transparency International reports.

nodes.label: Governments of the Georgian Dream
nodes.full: After the election of 1 October 2012, which Georgian Dream won with about 55 per cent in the first peaceful transfer of power at the ballot, the founder Bidzina Ivanishvili was prime minister until November 2013 and was followed by Irakli Garibashvili (2013–2015, 2021–2024), Giorgi Kvirikashvili, Mamuka Bakhtadze, Giorgi Gakharia and from February 2024 Irakli Kobakhidze. Ivanishvili, who had given up his office, remained honorary chairman, and critics describe him as the country's real ruler, while the party says he holds no executive power.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (2012–2024); OSCE/ODIHR reports.

nodes.label: Tbilisi war and western civil war
nodes.full: Armed groups of the National Guard and the Mkhedrioni, under Tengiz Kitovani and Jaba Ioseliani, rose against Gamsakhurdia on 22 December 1991; the fighting in the centre of Tbilisi damaged Rustaveli Avenue and ended on 6 January 1992 with his flight. His supporters, the Zviadists, held much of Mingrelia in the west, and in September–October 1993 the state's forces, helped by Russian transport and by the acceptance of Russian bases and membership in the CIS, defeated them at Zugdidi and Senaki.
nodes.src: Jones 2012; Suny 1994; Georgian press and memoir accounts.

nodes.label: War in Abkhazia
nodes.full: Georgian troops entered Abkhazia on 14 August 1992 after the Abkhaz parliament's restoration of its 1925 constitution in July 1992; the Abkhaz forces, aided by volunteers from the North Caucasus and by Russian military support, took Gagra in October and in September 1993 Sukhumi, in a fight that ended with the flight or expulsion of almost all of the Georgian population, some 200,000–250,000 people. The Georgian side speaks of aggression and ethnic cleansing, a term used by the OSCE summits of 1994 and 1996, while the Abkhaz side calls it the Patriotic War and defence of self-determination and cites Georgian violations in 1992–1993; a ceasefire was signed in Moscow on 14 May 1994.
nodes.src: OSCE Budapest (1994) and Lisbon (1996) declarations; Human Rights Watch, Georgia/Abkhazia (1995); Jones 2012.

nodes.label: War in South Ossetia
nodes.full: After the autonomous oblast's abolition by the Georgian parliament in December 1990 and a Soviet-era conflict, fighting between Georgian forces and Ossetian militias went on in 1991–1992 around Tskhinvali, with some 1,000 killed and tens of thousands of Ossetians and Georgians displaced; the Sochi agreement of 24 June 1992 set up a joint peacekeeping force of Georgian, Russian and Ossetian units and left the question of status open.
nodes.src: Sochi Agreement (24 June 1992); Human Rights Watch, Bloodshed in the Caucasus (1992); Jones 2012.

nodes.label: Attempts on Shevardnadze
nodes.full: On 29 August 1995 a car bomb exploded beside Shevardnadze's motorcade in Tbilisi, injuring him, and on 9 February 1998 an armed group attacked his convoy with grenades and rifles, killing members of his escort; Georgian authorities blamed Zviadist and security-service plotters, and the cases also showed the influence of the militias and the security services of the time.
nodes.src: Georgian court records; Jones 2012.

nodes.label: Rose Revolution
nodes.full: After the parliamentary election of 2 November 2003, which international observers found to fall short of standards and local observers found fraudulent, crowds led by Mikheil Saakashvili, Zurab Zhvania and Nino Burjanadze gathered daily, and on 22 November Saakashvili and his supporters entered the parliament holding roses, interrupting Shevardnadze's speech. He resigned the next day; the new elections of 4 January 2004 gave Saakashvili about 96 per cent.
nodes.src: OSCE/ODIHR report (2003); Jones 2012; Georgian press.

nodes.label: Return of Adjara
nodes.full: In the spring of 2004 the president of the autonomous republic of Adjara, Aslan Abashidze, who had ruled it with his own forces as a quasi-independent domain, blocked the president's visit and destroyed bridges to Batumi; after demonstrations in Batumi and a Russian-mediated agreement he left for Moscow on 6 May 2004, and the region returned to central control without bloodshed. The event was the model that Tbilisi wished to repeat in Abkhazia and South Ossetia.
nodes.src: Jones 2012; International Crisis Group, Saakashvili's Ajarian Success: Repeatable in Abkhazia? (2004).

nodes.label: Crackdown of November 2007
nodes.full: After a week of opposition rallies in front of the parliament against the government and Saakashvili, riot police used tear gas, rubber bullets and water cannon on 7 November, and the television station Imedi was raided and closed; a state of emergency was declared for nine days and the president called a snap election for 5 January 2008, which he won with about 53 per cent. International observers criticised the crackdown and the media situation.
nodes.src: OSCE/ODIHR report (2008); Human Rights Watch, Crossing the Line (2007).

nodes.label: War of August 2008
nodes.full: After weeks of rising tension and exchanges of fire, Georgian forces shelled Tskhinvali on the night of 7–8 August 2008, and Russian forces, which had entered through the Roki tunnel, advanced into Georgia proper as far as Gori and Poti, and Abkhaz forces took the Kodori Gorge; a ceasefire mediated by Nicolas Sarkozy was agreed on 12 August. The EU's fact-finding mission under Heidi Tagliavini concluded in 2009 that the open hostilities began with the Georgian shelling, that the build-up of tension had been the responsibility of both parties, and that Russia's response and the ethnic cleansing of Georgians in South Ossetia went beyond what was lawful. About 850 people were killed in all and some 138,000 were displaced; the Georgian and Russian narratives remain opposed.
nodes.src: Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Conflict in Georgia, Report (30 September 2009); Ronald Asmus, A Little War That Shook the World (2010).

nodes.label: Borderisation
nodes.full: After Russia recognised the two territories on 26 August 2008 and stationed bases there, the administrative boundary lines were fenced and marked by barbed wire and signs, often moved a few hundred metres into Georgian-controlled land; people have been detained for crossing, and Giga Otkhozoria in 2016 and Archil Tatunashvili in 2018 died in incidents which Georgia's parliament cited in a list of sanctions. Moscow, Sukhumi and Tskhinvali say the lines are state borders, and the Georgian government and the EU call it creeping annexation.
nodes.src: EU Monitoring Mission reports; Georgian Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements; Otkhozoria–Tatunashvili list (2019).

nodes.label: Protests of June 2019
nodes.full: The sitting of a Russian Duma deputy, Sergei Gavrilov, in the chair of the speaker at an inter-parliamentary Orthodox assembly in the Georgian parliament on 20 June 2019 brought thousands in front of the building, and the police used tear gas and rubber bullets on the night of 20–21 June, injuring some 240 people, among them two who lost an eye. The government promised proportional elections and Russia banned flights to Georgia.
nodes.src: Civil.ge and OSCE reports (June 2019); Public Defender's report.

nodes.label: Foreign-influence law protests
nodes.full: In March 2023 a bill on foreign agents, modelled on the Russian one, brought tens of thousands to the streets, and it was withdrawn on 9 March. The Georgian Dream reintroduced it as the law on transparency of foreign influence in April 2024; after weeks of protests it was passed on 14 May, vetoed by President Zourabichvili on 18 May and enacted by an override on 28 May. The government presents it as a defence of sovereignty and transparency, and the opposition, the EU and the United States as a copy of Russian practice.
nodes.src: Parliament of Georgia records (2023, 2024); Venice Commission opinion (2024); EU and US statements.

nodes.label: Elections of 2024 and protests
nodes.full: The election of 26 October 2024 gave Georgian Dream, by the official count, about 54 per cent and 89 seats; the opposition parties and Zourabichvili rejected the result and alleged vote buying, intimidation and a rigged system, and international observers noted irregularities and pressure, while the government said the election was valid. After Prime Minister Kobakhidze announced on 28 November that accession talks with the EU would be paused until 2028, nightly protests began on Rustaveli Avenue, with police using water cannon and tear gas and many arrests; the 4 October 2025 local elections ended with an attempt by protesters to enter the presidential palace, which the authorities treated as an attempt at a coup.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission and OSCE/ODIHR preliminary report (27 October 2024); statement of 28 November 2024; Civil.ge reports (2024–2025).

nodes.label: Restoration of independence
nodes.full: In a referendum on 31 March 1991 some 99 per cent of the voters, at a turnout of about 90 per cent, supported the restoration of Georgia's independence of 1918–1921, and on 9 April 1991 the Supreme Council adopted the Act of Restoration of State Independence, chosen for the anniversary of the shooting of 9 April 1989; the Soviet Union's dissolution was completed in December. The act's legal premise is that the Soviet occupation of 1921 was illegal and that independence had been restored.
nodes.src: Act of Restoration of State Independence (9 April 1991); referendum records.

nodes.label: Constitutions of 1995 and 2017
nodes.full: The constitution of 24 August 1995 created a strong presidency; the amendments of 2004, 2010 and 2017 moved the state to a mixed and then a parliamentary system under which, from 2024, the president is elected by an electoral college and the prime minister holds executive power. The 2017 revision also introduced a fully proportional system of elections from 2024.
nodes.src: Constitution of Georgia (1995, as amended); Venice Commission opinions.

nodes.label: Reforms of 2004–2012
nodes.full: The government of the Rose Revolution dismissed the traffic police of some 15,000 in 2004–2005, raised salaries in the administration, abolished many licences, simplified the taxes and customs, cut petty corruption drastically and in the World Bank's Doing Business ranking of the early 2010s was among the first fifteen economies; its critics point to the concentration of power, the abuse of the prison system and the use of plea bargains.
nodes.src: World Bank, Doing Business reports (2010–2013); Transparency International; Jones 2012.

nodes.label: Elections and their disputes
nodes.full: The OSCE/ODIHR assessed the elections of the 1990s as improving but flawed, that of November 2003 as falling short of the standards, the presidential election of 2008 as competitive but with serious problems and that of 2012 as a step toward consolidation; the parliamentary election of 31 October 2020 was found competitive but with misuse of resources and led to an opposition boycott until an EU-mediated agreement in 2021, which Georgian Dream later abandoned; and that of 26 October 2024 was disputed, as above.
nodes.src: OSCE/ODIHR election observation mission reports (1995–2024).

nodes.label: Russia’s recognition and treaties
nodes.full: On 26 August 2008 Russian president Medvedev recognised Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states, which Georgia, the EU, NATO and the UN General Assembly's majority did not accept; Nicaragua, Venezuela, Syria and Nauru followed. Russia signed a treaty of alliance and strategic partnership with Abkhazia on 24 November 2014 and one on alliance and integration with South Ossetia on 18 March 2015, and Georgia passed the law on occupied territories of 2008 and regards the two as territory occupied by Russia.
nodes.src: Presidential decrees of the Russian Federation (26 August 2008); treaties of 2014 and 2015; Law of Georgia on Occupied Territories (2008).

nodes.label: Family-values and FARA laws
nodes.full: The law on family values and the protection of minors of September 2024 restricts gender-affirming care, public advocacy and the legal recognition of same-sex relations, and the law on the registration of foreign agents of April 2025, modelled on the United States' FARA, together with amendments on grants and broadcasting, required organisations and media financed from abroad to register and report. The government describes them as the protection of traditional values and of sovereignty, and the EU, the Council of Europe and human-rights bodies as a restriction of civic space and discrimination.
nodes.src: Laws of Georgia (2024, 2025); Venice Commission and OSCE opinions; EU statements.

nodes.label: Constitutional Court party case
nodes.full: In October 2025 Georgian Dream filed a suit in the Constitutional Court to have the United National Movement, Lelo and the Coalition for Change declared unconstitutional as parties linked to Saakashvili's regime and to the boycott of parliament, later adding other groups; the party says it is a defence of the constitutional order, while the opposition and Western governments see an attempt to eliminate the opposition. As of October 2026 the court has not ruled, and under its rules it is due to decide by June 2027.
nodes.src: Constitutional Court of Georgia filings and press releases (2025–2026); Civil.ge and Interpressnews reports.

nodes.label: Ilia II and the Church
nodes.full: Catholicos-Patriarch Ilia II, in office since 1977, became the most trusted public figure in the country, and the Church acquired a constitutional agreement and concordat on 14 October 2002 with privileges in education and property and a public role; the Holy Trinity (Sameba) Cathedral in Tbilisi, begun in 1995, was consecrated on 23 November 2004. The Church's influence on public morality and politics has been seen by supporters as the guardian of identity and by critics as a conservative pressure on liberties.
nodes.src: Constitutional Agreement between the State of Georgia and the Georgian Apostolic Autocephalous Orthodox Church (2002); Jones 2012.

nodes.label: Attacks on minority faiths and 17 May 2013
nodes.full: From 1999 to 2003 groups led by the defrocked priest Basil Mkalavishvili attacked Jehovah's Witnesses, Baptists and others, with police inaction criticised by the European Court of Human Rights, and after the Rose Revolution he was convicted in 2005; on 17 May 2013 thousands led by priests and lay people broke through police lines and attacked a small march for the International Day against Homophobia in Tbilisi, and the case again raised the question of the state's and Church's tolerance.
nodes.src: European Court of Human Rights, Members of the Gldani Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses v. Georgia (2007); Human Rights Watch reports.

nodes.label: Death of Ilia II and Shio III
nodes.full: Ilia II died on 17 March 2026 at the age of 93 after nearly half a century as patriarch, and after a period in which Metropolitan Shio (Mujiri) served as locum tenens the Holy Synod elected Shio III as his successor in May 2026; observers expect a conservative patriarch whose relations with the government and with the Western churches will matter. As of October 2026 his policies are only beginning to be visible.
nodes.src: Georgian Orthodox Church statements (2026); Eurasianet, Crux and Civil.ge reports.

nodes.label: UNESCO listings
nodes.full: Georgian polyphonic singing was proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage in 2001 and inscribed in 2008, the traditional qvevri wine-making in 2013 and the three Georgian writing systems in 2016; the listings reflect the country's attention to the antiquity of its culture, among them the traces of wine-making in Neolithic villages of about 6000 BC announced in 2017.
nodes.src: UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage (2008, 2013, 2016).

nodes.label: Tangerines and And Then We Danced
nodes.full: Zaza Urushadze's Tangerines (2013), a film about two enemies in an Abkhaz village during the war of 1992, was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film; Levan Akin's And Then We Danced (2019), a love story between two men in a national dance company, was a success abroad and was met with protest at its screenings in Tbilisi and Batumi in November 2019.
nodes.src: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences records; press reports (2014–2019).

nodes.label: Chess and weightlifting
nodes.full: The Georgian women's chess tradition of Nona Gaprindashvili, the first woman grandmaster (1978), and Maia Chiburdanidze continued under the independent state, and the weightlifter Lasha Talakhadze won the Olympic super-heavyweight gold in 2016 and 2020 with world records, while Georgian rugby and wrestling have been national passions.
nodes.src: FIDE and IWF records; Olympic Committee results.

nodes.label: The European identity
nodes.full: On 27 April 1999 Zurab Zhvania told the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, on Georgia's accession, that he was Georgian and therefore European; the phrase became the motto of the Western orientation of the Rose Revolution and of the public consensus of the following two decades, in which surveys showed some 80 per cent support for EU membership and a majority for NATO membership. The constitution of 2017 states the aim of integration into the EU and NATO.
nodes.src: Council of Europe PACE records (27 April 1999); Caucasus Barometer and NDI surveys (2012–2024); Constitution of Georgia, article 78.

nodes.label: The sovereignist turn
nodes.full: After 2022 Georgian Dream's leaders, among them Ivanishvili and Kobakhidze, began to speak of a global party of war, of external attempts to open a second front against Russia and of the foreign-funded character of NGOs, and made national sovereignty and traditional values the party's language; critics say the argument serves to justify the turn from the EU path in the face of the constitutional aim and the public's wish, while the party says it seeks peace, pragmatism and equal partnership with the West.
nodes.src: Statements of Ivanishvili and Kobakhidze (2023–2026); Civil.ge and Carnegie analyses.

nodes.label: Stalin in Gori and the Soviet occupation
nodes.full: The Museum of the Soviet Occupation in Tbilisi, opened in 2006 and expanded after the war, presents the period from 1921 as an occupation and a series of repressions; in Gori, Stalin's birthplace, his statue in the central square was removed on the night of 25 June 2010 and the museum in the town, with its unreformed story of him, remained a place of controversy between the memory of the terror and the local pride.
nodes.src: Museum of Soviet Occupation; Georgian press (2010); Jones 2012.

nodes.label: Collapse and the lari
nodes.full: The economy fell by about two thirds between 1990 and 1994 in the war, the closure of the railway through Abkhazia, the breakdown of trade with the former Soviet republics and a hyperinflation of the coupon currency, and the introduction of the lari on 2 October 1995 by Shevardnadze's government, with IMF support, ended the inflation and started a slow recovery.
nodes.src: IMF and World Bank country reports (1993–1997); Jones 2012.

nodes.label: Shadow economy of the 1990s
nodes.full: The privatisation of enterprises and the energy sector in the 1990s was followed by chronic non-payment, power cuts in the winters of the nineties, a large shadow economy and the capture of the customs and taxes by officials and clans; the budget of the early 2000s was only about 15 per cent of the gross domestic product.
nodes.src: World Bank reports; Transparency International reports.

nodes.label: Russian embargo on wine
nodes.full: In March–May 2006 Russia banned the import of Georgian wine, of which Russia had taken about 80 per cent of the exports, and of Borjomi and other mineral waters, citing health standards; the government in Tbilisi called it political pressure, and the wine industry found markets in Poland, Ukraine, China and the West, with exports rising again after the lifting of the ban in 2013.
nodes.src: Rospotrebnadzor and Georgian ministry statements (2006); National Wine Agency data.

nodes.label: Growth of the 2020s
nodes.full: The economy grew by about 10 per cent in 2022 and above 7 per cent in 2023 and 2024 according to the official statistics, helped by tourism, transit, re-exports and the arrival after 2022 of more than a hundred thousand Russians and others from the former Soviet region, many of whom stayed, with strong rises in rents and the inflow of money; economists note the vulnerability of such growth to external conditions and to the political uncertainty.
nodes.src: Geostat and National Bank of Georgia data (2022–2024); IMF Article IV reports.

nodes.label: BTC pipeline and BTK railway
nodes.full: The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan oil pipeline, inaugurated in Baku on 25 May 2005 and reaching Ceyhan in 2006, the parallel South Caucasus gas pipeline and the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway, opened on 30 October 2017, turned Georgia into a transit route for Azerbaijani energy and for trade avoiding Russia and Iran; the projects were supported by the United States, Turkey and Azerbaijan and bypass Russia and Armenia.
nodes.src: BP and State Oil Company of Azerbaijan documents; Georgian Railway statements (2017).

nodes.label: Anaklia port
nodes.full: The plan of a deep-water port at Anaklia on the Black Sea, awarded in 2016 to a consortium of TBC Holding and the American firm Conti, was ended by the government in January 2020 after it said the consortium had not met its financial commitments, a decision criticised by the consortium and the opposition as political; in May 2024 a Chinese-led group won a new competition, and in July 2026 the government decided to keep the state in ownership and to use international contractors; as of the summer of 2026 the first-stage works were under way and the first phase was foreseen for 2029.
nodes.src: Georgian government statements (2020, 2024, 2026); Eurasianet reports.

nodes.label: Public Service Halls
nodes.full: The Public Service Hall in Tbilisi, opened in 2011 under the Saakashvili government as a single window for services such as registration of property, identity documents and licences, and its glass buildings in several towns were an internationally cited example of the reduction of petty corruption and are still used by Georgian Dream governments.
nodes.src: Ministry of Justice of Georgia; OECD and World Bank studies.

nodes.label: NATO and Bucharest
nodes.full: Georgia sent some 2,000 soldiers to Iraq, among the largest contingents, and troops to Afghanistan, and at the Bucharest summit of 3 April 2008 NATO declared that Georgia and Ukraine would become members without a membership action plan, a statement that Russia and some NATO members have interpreted differently; the application remains frozen as of 2026.
nodes.src: NATO Bucharest Summit Declaration (3 April 2008); Asmus 2010.

nodes.label: Association Agreement and paused accession
nodes.full: Georgia signed its Association Agreement with the EU on 27 June 2014, with the free trade area in force from 1 July 2016 and the visa-free travel from 28 March 2017; it applied for membership on 3 March 2022 and was given candidate status on 14 December 2023, but after the foreign-influence law and the elections of 2024 the Commission found the process stalled, the government paused the talks until 2028, and the EU suspended the visa facilitation for officials and in March 2026 the visa-free travel of holders of diplomatic and service passports, with further steps possible.
nodes.src: EU Association Agreement (2014); European Council conclusions (14 December 2023); European Commission decisions (2025–2026).

nodes.label: Russia and the Geneva talks
nodes.full: Georgia broke diplomatic relations with Russia on 29 August 2008 and left the CIS in 2009; since October 2008 the Geneva International Discussions, co-chaired by the EU, OSCE and UN, and since 2009 a mechanism for prevention of incidents on the line have met without agreement on the key questions, and the EU Monitoring Mission has been in the country since 1 October 2008. Under Georgian Dream trade and the direct flights, which Russia resumed on 15 May 2023, have partly recovered, with the 2008 occupation still unresolved.
nodes.src: Geneva International Discussions statements; EUMM Georgia; Georgian and Russian government statements.

nodes.label: Triangle with Turkey and Azerbaijan
nodes.full: The partnership with Azerbaijan and Turkey, based on the pipelines and the railway, and on regular trilateral meetings, is the basis of Georgia's regional position; Turkey is the main trading partner, and Georgia has stayed neutral between Armenia and Azerbaijan and hosts both minorities. The Georgian government welcomed the peace initialled in August 2025 and the proposed transit routes.
nodes.src: Trilateral declarations (2012–2025); Georgian Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements.

nodes.label: China and the free trade agreement
nodes.full: A free trade agreement with China, the first in the region, took effect on 1 January 2018, the first of China's with a country of the region, a strategic partnership was announced on 31 July 2023 and Chinese companies took part in the Anaklia competition of 2024; the United States, whose Megobari bill passed the House in 2025, has questioned the relationship, and by July 2026 the Chinese consortium was reported to have left the port project.
nodes.src: FTA text (2017); joint statement (31 July 2023); US Congress and Eurasianet reports (2025–2026).

nodes.label: The United States
nodes.full: The US–Georgia Charter on Strategic Partnership of January 2009 was the basis for defence cooperation, the Millennium Challenge Corporation compacts and the training programmes; in December 2024 the United States suspended the partnership after the elections and the pause of the EU talks, and in 2025 Congress considered sanctions and the Megobari bill, which says that the American relationship is with the Georgian people rather than its government.
nodes.src: US–Georgia Charter (2009); US State Department statements (December 2024); Congressional records (2025).

nodes.label: The displaced
nodes.full: Some 200,000–250,000 Georgians were displaced from Abkhazia in 1992–1993 and tens of thousands from the Tskhinvali region; in 2008 about 138,000 left their homes, most of them returning but some 35,000 unable to, and the displaced persons, who were housed in collective centres and later in new settlements, number several hundred thousand in the Georgian government's list as of the 2020s.
nodes.src: UNHCR and Georgian Ministry of Internally Displaced Persons figures; EU fact-finding mission report (2009).

nodes.label: Tbilisi flood and Shovi landslide
nodes.full: On 13–14 June 2015 the Vere river flooded the centre of Tbilisi, killing about twenty people and releasing animals from the zoo, and on 3 August 2023 a mud-flow in the mountain resort of Shovi in Racha killed more than thirty people; both are cited as the effects of heavy rain, building in risk areas and the changing climate.
nodes.src: Georgian Ministry of Internal Affairs and National Environmental Agency reports.

nodes.label: Covid-19
nodes.full: The first case was recorded on 26 February 2020; a state of emergency and lockdown followed in spring 2020, the health system was strained in the waves of the autumn of 2020 and 2021, and about 17,000 deaths were recorded officially by 2023 among a population of about 3.7 million, one of the higher rates in Europe.
nodes.src: National Centre for Disease Control of Georgia; WHO data.

nodes.label: Population
nodes.full: The population fell from about 5.4 million in the Soviet census of 1989 to some 3.7 million in the census of 2014, because of the emigration of the 1990s, the secession of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, and a fall in the birth rate; the ethnic minorities, who had been about 30 per cent in 1989, were about 13 per cent in 2014.
nodes.src: Soviet census (1989); National Statistics Office of Georgia, census (2014).

nodes.label: Women and the law
nodes.full: Nino Burjanadze, speaker of parliament, was acting president in 2003–2004 and 2007–2008, and Salome Zourabichvili became the first woman elected president in 2018; the law on the elimination of domestic violence of 2006 and its amendments, the gender quota for party lists adopted in 2020 and the rights of women are advanced by the organisations, though representation in parliament has stayed at about a fifth.
nodes.src: Parliament of Georgia records; UN Women and Council of Europe reports.

nodes.label: LGBT communities and 5 July 2021
nodes.full: After the attacks of 17 May 2013, a planned pride march on 5 July 2021 was cancelled when far-right groups attacked the organisers' office and some fifty journalists, and the cameraman Alexander Lashkarava, who was beaten, died on 11 July; the government of the day condemned the violence but the party leaders said the march was inappropriate, and the law of 2024 has been criticised by the EU as discriminatory, while the government describes it as protecting families and minors.
nodes.src: Public Defender of Georgia; Human Rights Watch and Council of Europe reports (2021–2024).

nodes.label: Armenians, Azerbaijanis, Meskhetian Turks
nodes.full: In the census of 2014 about 6 per cent of the population were Azerbaijanis, mostly in Kvemo Kartli, and about 4.5 per cent Armenians, mostly in Javakheti, with weaker knowledge of Georgian and fewer positions in the administration; the law on repatriation of 2007 allowed the descendants of the Meskhetian Turks, deported in 1944, to apply for a return, but only a small number had resettled by the 2020s.
nodes.src: National Statistics Office of Georgia, census (2014); Law of Georgia on Repatriation (2007); OSCE High Commissioner reports.

nodes.label: Journalists and protesters arrested
nodes.full: In the protests of 2024–2025 several hundred people were detained and new administrative and criminal penalties for blocking roads were introduced; among those imprisoned was the Batumi journalist Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of Batumelebi and Netgazeti, who was sentenced on 6 August 2025 to two years for striking a police chief during a protest, a verdict that press-freedom organisations call disproportionate and the authorities describe as the application of the law.
nodes.src: Court records; Public Defender, Committee to Protect Journalists and Civil.ge reports (2025).

nodes.label: Migrant workers and remittances
nodes.full: Several hundred thousand Georgians have worked abroad in Russia, Greece, Italy, Turkey and in Israel as builders, caregivers and in services since the 1990s, and the remittances, which have been around ten per cent of the gross domestic product or more in the 2020s, sustain many families in the provinces; the arrivals after 2022 of tens of thousands of Russians, Ukrainians and Belarusians made Tbilisi and Batumi a destination too.
nodes.src: National Bank of Georgia remittance data; IOM and World Bank reports.

nodes.label: The national movement and the first conflicts
nodes.full: The Georgian national movement, the shooting of 9 April 1989, the Sukhumi events of July 1989 and the abolition of South Ossetia’s autonomous oblast in December 1990 prepared the independence acts and the conflicts of the 1990s.
nodes.src: background — see the Soviet Caucasus 1953–1991 folio (caucasus-1953-1991)

nodes.label: The Red Army’s entry in 1921
nodes.full: The entry of the Red Army into Tbilisi on 25 February 1921 ended the independent republic of 1918–1921, whose restoration the act of 1991 declared.
